sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Given a set of LEGO parts and an image of an assembled object, our task is to infer the pose of each part to assemble the object. In contrast with traditional 3D reconstruction, doing so requires satisfying discrete physical constraints, which provide structure but render the problem combinatorial and highly sensitive to small pose errors. To learn a prior over how parts fit together, we train a set-conditioned SE(3) flow model on procedurally generated assemblies. We then finetune this model to inject image conditioning, using 1% as much data. However, while the learned flow captures global structure, it does not enforce connectivity. To address this, we introduce an analytic connectivity-field guidance to pull predictions toward connected assemblies at test time. Through this, we demonstrate improved build quality with model size, pretraining, and guidance. We make our models and data available for research purposes at https://kulits.github.io/BrickFlow/

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Imagine opening new set of LEGO to find box full of pieces, but no instructions. All you have is the picture on the front of the box. You can identify number of parts visible on the surface, but the image only reveals the outside. The internal structure must be inferred: which bricks support which, 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). what fills the spaces you cannot see. Every piece must end up with precise position and orientation satisfying discrete connector-defined constraints. This is the problem we address: given an inventory of parts and single image of the completed assembly, recover the 6D pose of each piece (see Fig. 1). While sharing some of the ambiguities of traditional monocular 3D reconstruction such as from occlusion the task presents unique challenges. Though it is possible to computationally verify the validity of given assembly, figuring out how to go from parts to structure requires understanding not just how pieces fit together, but how they fit together jointly, over possibly many at once. Contributing to this complexity, our assembly domain spans thousands of parts which connect in diverse ways. We address this by learning partset-conditioned generative assembly prior. To obtain sufficient supervision, we generate large-scale procedural structure data using typed connector system [Kulits and Schmid, 2026] defined over LDraw [Jessiman, 19952026] parts, starting from randomly sampled pieces and iteratively placing new ones through compatible connectors. We use these to train an SE(3) flow model that takes an unordered inventory together with noisy poses and removes noise. The purpose of this stage is not to understand object semantics, but to learn the geometry of assembly: which parts can connect, how they tend to align, and how local connections compose into global structure. Rather than being human-designed or semantically meaningful, these assemblies provide constraint-rich samples from the physical grammar of LEGO assembly. Pretraining on this data amortizes search over connector-valid configurations into reusable prior on assembly and structure. We then adapt the assembly prior to perform partset-conditioned visual reconstruction. For this, we render smaller set of procedural assemblies to create structureimage pairs. From the images, we extract features from frozen visual encoder and finetune the flow model with injected cross-attention. Although pretraining captures useful global assembly structure, learned predictions alone do not guarantee precise connectivity. Small translational and rotational errors can leave intended connections slightly misaligned. To address this, we introduce connectivity-field guidance, an analytic test-time energy defined over poses and connector geometry. The field is zero on exactly connected assemblies, and its gradient pulls predictions toward connected structure. Following diffusion posterior sampling (DPS) [Chung et al., 2023], we condition on connectedness with the field as the negative log-likelihood, correcting poses in late steps along its gradient at the models predicted final assembly. We evaluate our model on both inventory-conditioned assembly and image-conditioned reconstruction. Beyond pose accuracy, we evaluate assembly and connection validity. We demonstrate that assembly pretraining improves structural understanding, that task performance scales with model capacity, and that connectivity-field guidance improves the validity of assemblies when applied at inference time. Our core contributions are as follows: 1. We train set-conditioned SE(3) flow model on procedurally generated LEGO assemblies to learn an adaptable assembly prior 2. We adapt this prior to single-image reconstruction using fraction the amount of data 3. We introduce connectivity-field guidance, an analytic energy that injects known connector structure at test time, pulling predictions toward connected assemblies without retraining

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Brick Assembly. Prior work on brick assembly has addressed several specific subproblems. Legolization methods convert target geometry into brick layouts on discrete grids [Luo et al., 2015, Lennon et al., 2021]. BrickGPT [Pun et al., 2025] finetunes language model to autoregressively place bricks, but predicts voxel positions over small block vocabulary; LEGO-Maker [Ge et al., 2025] creates LEGO models from an image over similarly restricted part set. For reconstruction, Tattersall et al. [2020] recover LEGO models from 24 calibrated views via space carving and cuboid fitting, but handle only four rectangular brick types; Wang et al. [2022] infer per-step brick poses from instruction manuals but address sequential single-part placement rather than joint assembly. BrickNet [Kulits and Schmid, 2026] introduce typed connector system and graph-based generation over the full LDraw part library and finetune language model to autoregressively produce brick structures from text. Each step places part through connection to the existing structure, so its outputs are connected by construction, and it takes no image or inventory. BrickBench [Kulits et al., 2026] evaluates coding agents on text-conditioned design of buildable assemblies with up to 4000 parts using the same library 2 and tests them under different constraints. Apart from the per-step placement of Wang et al. [2022], these methods choose which parts to use, and none is provided fixed set of parts. Providing an inventory constrains the structure without determining it, as the same parts can build many assemblies. As it must be used exactly, model cannot omit part that does not fit and must connect every part. No prior work addresses inventory-conditioned assembly or reconstruction over the full part library. 3D Part Assembly. Generative part assembly methods predict rigid poses for set of parts to form complete object [Huang et al., 2020, Li et al., 2020], with recent work using score-based [Cheng et al., 2023], diffusion [Scarpellini et al., 2024, Zhao et al., 2025], hierarchical [Du et al., 2024], and flow-based [Li et al., 2025, Sun et al., 2025] formulations. GARF [Li et al., 2025] and Rectified Point Flow [Sun et al., 2025] are 3D-only, though Assembler [Zhao et al., 2025] is additionally image-conditioned. While these are architecturally similar (we employ standard DiT [Peebles and Xie, 2023]), they differ in task, and are designed for arbitrary geometry encoded as sampled points. SE(3) Flow Matching and Guided Sampling. The flow matching paradigm [Lipman et al., 2023, Liu et al., 2023] has been extended to SE(3) for protein structure generation [Bose et al., 2024, Yim et al., 2023, Campbell et al., 2024], where, as in our setting, structures are built from fixed vocabulary of units rather than arbitrary parts. Diffusion posterior sampling (DPS) [Chung et al., 2023] corrects each denoising step using gradients of measurement likelihood; classifier [Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021] and classifier-free [Ho and Salimans, 2021] guidance follow the same principle with learned signals. Our connectivity-field guidance applies the DPS correction with an analytic energy over known connector geometry as the negative log-likelihood. No prior work integrates connectivity differentiably as test-time guidance in an assembly task.

sections.title: 3.1 Modeling
sections.content: We represent LEGO assemblies using the LDraw [Jessiman, 19952026] modeling system, which consists of digital replicas of thousands of parts. In LDraw, model is defined by set of piece instances, each having type, material, and SE(3) pose. It does not directly model part connectivity, for which we employ the BrickNet [Kulits and Schmid, 2026] typed connector system, an annotation layer of local connector frames over LDraw parts which defines how pieces connect to one another. These connection interfaces include studhole, hinge, axle, ball joint, and fixed connectors, each defining family of allowed relative transforms between two parts. Stud-type connectors, for instance, allow for one degree of rotational freedom about an interface. Given an LDraw assembly, BrickNet parses posed parts into graph where structure is defined by pieces as nodes and edges of connectivity. In this work, we use LDraw as the source of part geometry, while the BrickNet connector system is used to evaluate the validity of an assembly and integral to the production of procedural training data.

sections.title: 3.2 ProcBrick
sections.content: To train our assembly prior, we introduce ProcBrick, procedural generator of LEGO assemblies, and use it to synthesize dataset of 100 million structures of 100 parts each. Parts are drawn from 6,339 geometry classes, which we use to group LDraw parts with identical colliders and connector interfaces. Starting with random seed piece, we iteratively append pieces onto the structure. Rather than sample naively in space, we attempt placements at random compatible connector sites and reject those that collide. However, naive rejection sampling favors sparse assemblies: placements that extend into open space rarely collide, while those among existing parts, where further connections would form, do so more frequently. We instead stochastically accept collision-free placements to favor dense packing and, for each new part, numbers of connector joins and connected neighbors within the range of human-designed models, so that assemblies are compact and multiply connected. As sampling is autoregressive, each sequence prefix defines valid structure and lengths can be varied in pretraining. For image-conditioned finetuning, we generate an additional one million ProcBrick structures, 1% as many as for pretraining, and render them with Blender. Rather than consistently include 100 parts, we balance counts between 2 and 100. For rendering, each part is assigned printed or plain variant of its geometry class and material, giving 12,663 distinct parts. We fit part and material frequencies to human-designed models (see Sec. H). See Fig. 2 for render samples. Although the procedural assemblies are not individually realistic as sets human might construct, our intent is not to model semantics but to span the space of valid structure to achieve broad support. 3 Figure 2: ProcBrick samples. We provide sample renders from ProcBrick of increasing complexity. The observable differences in shading are due to random HDRI selection done at the time of rendering.

sections.title: 3.5 Architecture
sections.content: We use standard diffusion-transformer (DiT) [Peebles and Xie, 2023] backbone without SE(3)- equivariant layers  (Fig. 3)  . Prior work on SE(3) flow matching for proteins [Yim et al., 2024] uses invariant point attention (IPA) layers from AlphaFold 2 [Jumper et al., 2021], but with data augmentation, non-equivariant models can match the data efficiency of equivariant ones given sufficient training [Brehmer et al., 2025]; AlphaFold 3 [Abramson et al., 2024] achieves strong results with non-equivariant architecture and data augmentation, which we follow. Each input token represents part: the token embedding is the sum of learned part-type embedding, linear encodings of the current pose, and optionally learned material embedding. As the input is unordered, no positional encoding is used. In the reconstruction experiment, we inject image conditioning through decoupled cross-attention [Ye et al., 2023] in each of the DiT blocks from part tokens to frozen DINOv3-L [Siméoni et al., 2025] features (CLS and patch tokens) from layer 18 of 24, compressed by Perceiver resampler [Jaegle et al., 2021, Alayrac et al., 2022]. keypoint head additionally predicts where each parts center of mass projects into the image, trained with β-NLL loss [Seitzer et al., 2022]. We drop the image for 10% of training examples and sample with classifier-free guidance [Ho and Salimans, 2021] of strength 2, handing off to the pretrained model for the final steps (t 0.85).

sections.title: 3.6 Connectivity Field
sections.content: While large-scale pretraining teaches the model useful global assembly prior, the learned flow does not explicitly enforce connector alignment. Small positional errors or drifts can leave two parts misaligned, leading to an assembly where the predicted structure might be qualitatively close, but disconnected. This is natural failure mode for direct pose prediction in SE(3)N : the set of connector-consistent configurations has measure zero in the full space. To address this, we introduce connectivity-field guidance, scalar energy defined over joint pose whose gradient nudges estimates toward connected configurations. We apply it at test time during sampling. sections.title: 4.1 Setup
sections.content: Models. We pretrain inventory-conditioned DiT-S/B/L (PT) on 100M procedural assemblies. For image-conditioned (IC) reconstruction, we finetune each on 1M rendered assemblies (Tab. 2). For ablations, we additionally train IC DiT-S from random initialization and ablate the amount of data. Evaluation sets. We evaluate on 9,900 held-out ProcBrick assemblies, 100 for each part count from 2 to 100, and on the 512 models of the BrickNet [Kulits and Schmid, 2026] validation set, with 512512 input images. We draw 100 samples. DPS uses connectivity-field guidance (Sec. 3.7). Metrics. Pose error alone does not show whether an assembly holds together, so we report connectivity and collisions alongside it. Valid: BrickNets connectivity and collision checks [Kulits and Schmid, 2026], applied to the whole assembly rather than per build step: the parsed connector graph has one component and no two parts collide by more than 1.1 LDU (); BrickNets default of 1.0 LDU gives nearly identical results (Tab. 5). Comp. and Max comp.: number of connected components () and size of the largest one (). MM (mass movement): root-mean-square material displacement (Eq. (3)) to the ground truth in LDU, with every part weighted equally, after optimal global alignment and symmetry-aware assignment of interchangeable parts (). Coll.: colliding part pairs per sample (). We report 95% confidence intervals from bootstrap over structures. 4.2 Image-Conditioned Reconstruction Tab. 1 summarizes reconstruction quality across both evaluation sets. Validity scales with model size: on BrickNet, unguided IC DiT-S/B/L reach 19.4%, 26.1%, and 30.5%, and guidance adds 4.65.6 points at every size. PT models scale likewise on BrickNet, from 13.6% to 25.5% (Tab. 5). Image conditioning reduces pose error, lowering MM from 58.9 to 31.0 LDU on BrickNet (PT DiT-L to IC DiT-L). ProcBrick follows the same trends at lower validity, as its assemblies are on average twice as large. Finetuning on 50% or 25% of the renders lowers the BrickNet validity of IC DiT-S only moderately, from 19.4% to 18.1% and 16.2% (Sec. G). Training IC DiT-S without the pretrained model, from random initialization and without the hand-off, lowers MM but increases the number of components and lowers BrickNet validity from 19.4% to 2.3% (Sec. sections.title: 4.3 Connectivity and Guidance
sections.content: Without guidance, the number of components grows with part count  (Fig. 5)  . Guidance reduces it at every part count, roughly halving it for the largest assemblies. Guidance changes MM by at most 0.3 LDU (Tab. 5). Guided samples also have fewer colliding pairs than unguided ones for every model (Tab. 1). Validity nonetheless falls with part count, with or without guidance, to below 1% beyond about 50 parts for single samples and beyond 85 parts for the best of 100. Large samples keep most parts in one component, but single detached part or collision makes sample invalid.

sections.content: Reconstruction examples on BrickNet are shown in Fig. 6. The model recovers visible structure and infers plausible placements for occluded parts. Fig. 7 shows reconstructions from photographs of physical builds, given their part inventories. 8 n p Figure 7: Real-world reconstructions. Inputs are photographs of physical builds. Outputs are from guided IC DiT-L, and are rendered following postprocessing global alignment to set the camera.

sections.title: 5 Discussion and Limitations
sections.content: While the connectivity-field guidance improves connectivity substantially, it does not guarantee fully connected or physically valid assemblies. The field has no explicit collision term, so it reduces collisions only indirectly, by pulling parts into seats. Achieving full validity may require better test-time optimization, for example with explicit collision terms or discrete search over possibilities. While our synthetic data appears to cover the test distribution fairly well, the model struggles in dense builds where parts look alike  (Fig. 6)  . We suspect performance is limited by the distribution gap. We assume that the inventory contains exactly the parts of the depicted assembly, and the method is not trained to handle missing, extra, or wrong parts. Future work might consider how to handle this, but should consider more strongly the much more interesting problem of jointly inferring the objects partset along with the poses of the parts. To make the method applicable to images captured in-the-wild, where the partset is not already known, such as to digitize LEGO collection, interested readers might look to how co-generation is done in protein-generation literature such as in Campbell et al. [2024] with mixed continuousdiscrete denoising. Finally, while we train on assemblies of up to 100 parts, real-world LEGO sets can contain thousands. Scaling to larger assemblies will require addressing both computational cost and the increased ambiguity of inferring large hidden substructures from single view.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: Our work represents the first attempt to reconstruct LEGO object given an image and its set of parts. To achieve this, we first trained set-conditioned SE(3) flow model on procedurally generated assemblies (ProcBrick) to learn an adaptable assembly prior. Second, we adapted this prior to singleimage reconstruction using fraction of the data, and despite training only on renders, demonstrated that the resulting model can produce plausible reconstructions of physical builds from photographs. Finally, we introduced connectivity-field guidance, test-time energy that pulls predictions toward connected assemblies during sampling, applicable without retraining, raising validity for every model at negligible pose cost and halving the number of disconnected components in large assemblies.

sections.title: H ProcBrick Details
sections.content: Generation. placement is rejected if two parts interpenetrate by more than 1 LDU, unless they are joined by fixed connection. Part-type frequencies are tilted toward larger parts and calibrated per connector family. The seed part follows the occurrence frequencies of part types in humandesigned models. The acceptance test penalizes drops in packing density, and its targets for connector joins and connected neighbors per added part span roughly the median to the upper quantiles of human-designed models. Splits. All 100M pretraining assemblies pass the BrickNet collision check on every prefix. From separate pool, we draw disjoint sets of 1M image-training, 9,900 evaluation, and 1,000 geometryvalidation assemblies. Appearance and rendering. Each parts material is one of 260 renderer materials, drawn by policy fitted to the palettes of 53,431 human-designed models. We render at 10241024 on transparent background, lit by one of 964 environment maps or, for 10% of images, studio setup. During finetuning, we composite renders onto ImageNet [Deng et al., 2009] or plain backgrounds and apply random camera roll, zoom, and offset, random erasing, photometric jitter, and sensor noise.
